Tapu (the source, via Captain Cook, of the English word taboo ) is the sacred-forbidden: the state of being so charged with the sacred that contact is dangerous and restricted. The two are inseparable — what has great mana is tapu — and together they ordered all of life, from the chief's person to the preparation of food; the violation of an important tapu could be punishable by death . Society was ranked by mana: the ariki (chiefs) held it by descent from the gods, and the tohunga (Hawaiian kahuna ), the priest-experts, knew how to wield and contain it. The gods and the world-parents Polynesian creation begins, in the classic Māori account, with Rangi , the Sky Father, and Papa , the Earth Mother, locked in embrace in the darkness, until their children force them apart to let in the light and make the world (the world-parent cosmogony of ch46). From them come the great gods, worshipped across Polynesia under related names: Tangaroa (Hawaiian Kanaloa ), god of the sea; Tāne ( Kāne ), god of forests, birds, and light; Tū ( Kū ), god of war; and Rongo ( Lono ), god of agriculture and peace. Beloved above all is Māui , the trickster-hero who fished up the islands from the sea, snared the sun to slow it, and died seeking immortality for humankind. Regional deities loom large — the Hawaiian volcano goddess Pele , beautiful and destroying. Worship centered on the open sacred precinct, the marae (Hawaiian heiau ), with offerings, chant, feasting, and — in some societies — human sacrifice to the war-god. Rapa Nui: the ancestors in stone Rapa Nui developed a self-contained Polynesian religious world of…

title: Pentecostalism & Global Christianity
summary: The fire and the southern shift — the fastest-growing movement in modern religion, and the transformation of Christianity into a Global-South faith. The Azusa Street Revival (1906) under William Seymour and the Holiness roots (Parham, 1901); the baptism in the Holy Spirit and the restored gifts — speaking in tongues, prophecy, and divine healing, modeled on Acts 2; the three waves (classical Pentecostal denominations, the 1960s Charismatic movement into the mainline and Catholic churches, and the neo-charismatic independents); the prosperity gospel, reported honestly and contested; and the demographic shift of the Christian majority to Africa, Latin America, and Asia. A symbology of the tongues of fire, the raised hands, and the laying on of hands — an aniconic Christianity of direct experience, with its theological claims marked as faith.
text: In April 1906, in a run-down former Methodist church on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, something broke loose that would remake world Christianity. Led by William J. Seymour , the one-eyed son of former slaves, a crowd of Black, white, Latino, and Asian worshippers prayed, wept, sang, fell to the floor, and — most astonishingly to onlookers — spoke in tongues , uttering syllables they believed the Holy Spirit was giving them directly. The revival ran day and night for three years and sent missionaries around the globe. From that stable-like mission grew the fastest-growing religious movement of the modern age. The third force Pentecostalism is often called the " third force " in Christianity, standing alongside Catholicism and Protestantism as a distinct stream — and today the most dynamic of the three. Born at the very start of the 20th century, it has grown from almost nothing to some 600 million adherents (counting the wider charismatic movement), and it is the leading edge of the single greatest shift in modern religion: the movement of Christianity's center of gravity from the West to the Global South . The fire falls Pentecostalism grew out of the 19th-century Holiness movement , itself rooted in John Wesley's teaching of a " second blessing " of sanctification after conversion. The Holiness preacher Charles Fox Parham , at his Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, in 1901 , taught that there was a further, "third" experience — a baptism in the Holy Spirit — and that its biblical evidence was speaking in tongues . His student William J. Seymour carried the teaching to Los Angeles, where in 1906 the Azusa Street Revival ignited. What made Azusa historic was not only the ecstatic experience but its interracial character — extraordinary for its time (a Black pastor leading whites and Blacks together, though the interracial unity soon fractured under the pressures of a segregated society) — and its missionary energy, which broadcast the movement worldwide within a few years. Seymour chronicled it in a periodical, The Apostolic Faith . The baptism in the Spirit The heart of Pentecostalism is the conviction that the gifts of the Holy Spirit described in the New Testament — the charismata of 1 Corinthians 12 — are available to believers today , not confined to the apostolic past. Central is the baptism in the Holy Spirit , a direct, overwhelming experience of God typically evidenced by glossolalia (speaking in tongues), modeled on the first Pentecost in Acts 2, when the Spirit descended on the disciples as tongues of fire and they spoke in other languages. With it come the other gifts: prophecy , divine healing , miracles, and the discernment and casting-out of spirits. Pentecostalism is, above all, a religion of direct, felt, ecstatic experience of the divine — not primarily creed, sacrament, or institution, but the living presence of the Spirit, now. Three waves The movement spread in three great waves. Classical Pentecostalism built new denominations — the Assemblies of God , the largely African-American Church of God in Christ , and many more. Then, from the 1960s , the Charismatic movement carried the gifts into the existing churches : Spirit…

title: Bahá'í & New Faiths
summary: One God, one religion, one humanity — the archive’s closing chapter, on the faith that tries to hold all the others in a single embrace. The Bahá'í Faith: the Báb (executed 1850) and Bahá'u’lláh (1817–1892), exiled to ʾAkká; the three onenesses and the doctrine of progressive revelation, which gathers Abraham, Krishna, Moses, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Báb, and Bahá'u’lláh into one unfolding succession of Manifestations; the strikingly modern social teachings (equality of the sexes, harmony of science and religion, world peace); a clergy-less order under the Universal House of Justice in Haifa; and the systematic persecution of Bahá’ís in Iran. Plus the wider modern ‘new world faiths’ — Caodaism, the Ahmadiyya, Tenrikyo. A symbology of the nine-pointed star, the Greatest Name, and the terraced mountain — with progressive revelation flagged as the faith’s own framework, not neutral history.
text: In July 1850, in the Persian city of Tabriz, a young man who called himself the Báb — "the Gate" — was suspended by ropes before a firing squad of 750 soldiers. The first volley, it is said, cut his ropes and left him unharmed; when the smoke cleared he had vanished, found back in his cell finishing a conversation. A second regiment was brought; the second volley killed him. He was thirty. He had proclaimed that a new messenger of God was about to appear — and out of the movement he founded grew what may be the only major independent world religion born in the modern age: the Bahá'í Faith , whose whole purpose is to declare that all religions are one. A faith for a united world The Bahá'í Faith rests on three "onenesses": the oneness of God , the oneness of religion , and the oneness of humanity . It teaches that there is one God, unknowable in essence; that all the great religions come from that one God and form a single unfolding story; and that humankind is one family, now come of age and destined for unity. It is at once one of the youngest of the world's religions and one of the most geographically widespread, with communities in virtually every country on earth. The Báb and Bahá'u'lláh The faith has two founding figures. The Báb (Siyyid ʿAlí Muḥammad, 1819–1850), a merchant of Shiraz, declared in 1844 that he was the herald of one greater than himself, and his Bábí movement spread rapidly through Persia — and was savagely persecuted, with thousands of followers killed and the Báb himself executed in 1850. Among the Bábís was Bahá'u'lláh (Mírzá Ḥusayn-ʿAlí, 1817–1892), a Persian nobleman who, in 1863, declared that he was the one the Báb had foretold — the promised Manifestation of God for this age. Exiled by the Persian and Ottoman authorities ever farther from home — to Baghdad, Constantinople, Adrianople, and at last to the prison-city of ʿAkká (Acre) in Ottoman Palestine — he spent the rest of his life a prisoner, writing the enormous body of scripture on which the faith is built. It is from ʿAkká and neighboring Haifa , on Mount Carmel , that the Bahá'í world center grew, its golden-domed Shrine of the Báb and terraced gardens now among the most famous sights of the region. Progressive revelation The intellectual heart of the Bahá'í Faith is the doctrine of progressive revelation . God, it teaches, has never left humanity without guidance, but has sent a succession of Manifestations of God — Divine Educators — each renewing religion for a new age and preparing the way for the next, roughly every five hundred to a thousand years. Among these Manifestations Bahá'ís count Abraham, Krishna, Moses, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Báb, and Bahá'u'lláh . Each brought the same eternal truth in the form suited to their time and people; the apparent conflicts between religions are differences of social teaching fitted to different ages, not of essential truth. And the process has no end: future Manifestations will come. In this single framework the Bahá'í Faith attempts to gather the entire religious history this archive has surveyed into one continuous, divinely-guided story — an audacious and characteristically modern claim. title: The Voynich Manuscript
summary: A fifteenth-century vellum book in an unknown script that no one has been able to read — radiocarbon-dated, its owners traced from Rudolf II's Prague, and every proposed 'solution' tested and found wanting. Study all of Yale's page scans at full resolution, load the standard transliteration, and test a decipherment of your own.
text: Vault entry V01 · Manuscripts & Codices · Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University, MS 408 · Recently added — pending full review. A small book, about the size of a modern hardback (roughly 23 by 16 centimetres), lies in a climate-controlled vault in New Haven. It is bound in limp vellum. Inside are roughly 240 surviving pages of calfskin covered in a flowing, confident script that nobody alive, and as far as anyone can prove nobody dead, has ever been able to read. Beside the writing are plants that match no plant exactly, circles of stars and naked women, a zodiac with Latin-alphabet month names added by a later hand, green pools linked by tubes, and a folding sheet of nine rosettes joined by causeways. The book is catalogued as Beinecke MS 408, "Cipher manuscript". Everyone else calls it the Voynich Manuscript, after the antiquarian bookseller who brought it to light in 1912. This entry sets out what can be documented about the object (its material, its date, its owners, its structure) and keeps that apart from what has been claimed about it. Many people claim to have solved it, and each claim is examined below. The page scans on this entry come live from Yale's own image server. You can magnify any folio, sharpen faded ink, cut out a region at full resolution, and load the standard scholarly transliteration to test a decipherment of your own. The manuscript is a codex of vellum (calfskin) leaves gathered into quires. The quires carry their own numbering, and the gaps in that numbering show that some leaves are missing. Several leaves are foldouts, the largest of them the multi-panel sheet usually called the "Rosettes" page. The text is written in iron-gall-type brown ink. The drawings are outlined in the same ink and coloured with paints that are often thought to have been added later and less carefully than the outlines. The foliation (the folio numbers "f1r", "f68r3" and so on, used by everyone who works on it) was added afterwards in Arabic numerals. That is why modern references use foliation rather than page numbers. In 2009 the University of Arizona radiocarbon laboratory, working with Yale, dated four samples of the vellum from different leaves. The results were mutually consistent: the animals whose skins made the parchment died between 1404 and 1438 at 95% confidence. That dates the parchment, not necessarily the writing. In principle old blank vellum could be written on later, and some sceptics have argued exactly that. Ink and paint analyses made around the same time (reported by McCrone Associates) found nothing inconsistent with that period. Most specialists now treat an early-fifteenth-century origin for the book as the working assumption, and the date rules out older theories outright: Roger Bacon (d. 1292) cannot be the author, even though that attribution drove interest in the book for most of the twentieth century. The chain of ownership is unusually well documented for a medieval book, but it is not complete: - Before c. 1600, nothing is known. Where and by whom the book was made is entirely inferred. - Jacobus Horčický de Tepenec (d. 1622), a chemist and physician in Prague, signed the first folio. The…

title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
summary: Some 900–1,000 manuscripts from eleven caves near Qumran — the oldest copies of the Hebrew Bible, lost scriptures like Enoch and Jubilees, a sect's rules and war-liturgy, cryptic alphabets, a treasure list on copper — and the forgeries that followed them onto the market.
text: Vault entry V02 · Manuscripts & Codices · Israel Antiquities Authority and The Israel Museum, Jerusalem (with smaller holdings elsewhere) · Recently added — pending full review. In the winter of 1946–47 a Bedouin shepherd of the Ta'amireh tribe threw a stone into a cave in the cliffs above the north-western shore of the Dead Sea, heard pottery break, and later climbed in. Inside were tall clay jars. In the jars were leather scrolls wrapped in linen. One of them, taken out of that cave (now called Qumran Cave 1), was a copy of the Book of Isaiah seven metres long, complete from its first chapter to its sixty-sixth. It was about a thousand years older than any Hebrew manuscript of Isaiah scholars had held before. Over the next decade, Bedouin searchers and archaeologists found eleven caves around the ruin of Khirbet Qumran. Between them they held the remains of roughly 900–1,000 manuscripts, most of them broken into tens of thousands of fragments. This entry covers what the scrolls are, what they contain, how they have been read, and how they have been faked. It sets the documented archaeology apart from the theories built on top of it, the most debated being the question of who collected them. Strictly, the name means the manuscripts from the eleven Qumran caves. It is often stretched to cover finds from other Judaean Desert sites, including Masada, Wadi Murabba'at and Nahal Hever. Those finds are real and important, but they are separate deposits with different histories. Many are later, from the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132–135 CE. This entry keeps them apart. - Materials. Most scrolls are parchment (animal skin). A minority are papyrus. One, the Copper Scroll (3Q15), is text hammered into sheets of copper. - Languages and scripts. The great majority are in Hebrew, a substantial number in Aramaic, and a few in Greek. Most are written in the square "Jewish" script, some in the older palaeo-Hebrew script, and a handful in cryptic scripts (see Symbology below). - Date range. On palaeographic and radiocarbon grounds, the scrolls run from about the third century BCE to the first century CE. The caves are generally thought to have been sealed or abandoned around the Roman destruction of the Qumran site in c. 68 CE. The oldest biblical manuscripts. About a quarter of the Qumran manuscripts are copies of books later collected in the Hebrew Bible. Fragments have been identified for every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. Some books survive only as scraps, and the identification of some fragments is debated. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ), about 7.3 m long, 54 columns on 17 sheets, is the only book preserved complete. It is usually dated to roughly 150–100 BCE on palaeography, with radiocarbon ranges that overlap and extend earlier. A plural text, not one fixed Bible. The scrolls show that in the late Second Temple period the text of scripture was not yet fixed to one form. Many copies stand close to the later Masoretic Text. Others agree with the Greek Septuagint or with the Samaritan Pentateuch against it. 4QJerᵇ has the shorter Jeremiah known from the Septuagint. 4QSamᵃ preserves a passage about the Ammonite king Nahash at 1 Samuel 11 that is…

title: The Emerald Tablet
summary: Fourteen lines that became the scripture of European alchemy — 'that which is below is like that which is above.' Traced from the Arabic Book of the Secret of Creation to Newton's own translation, with the Latin and a line-by-line working translation, and kept apart from Doreal's 20th-century 'Tablets of Thoth.'
text: Vault entry V03 · Texts & Tablets · No physical tablet is known; the text survives in Arabic and Latin manuscripts and early printed books · Recently added — pending full review. The story comes before the text. A seeker, called Balīnūs in the Arabic sources (the name stands for Apollonius of Tyana, the first-century wonder-worker), goes down into a vault beneath a statue of Hermes. There he finds an old man seated on a golden throne, holding a tablet of green stone. On it, in a script the seeker can read, is written a short, strange text about the "one thing" from which all things come. That is the frame in which the Emerald Tablet (Tabula Smaragdina) first appears in writing. It is a tablet inside a story. No archaeologist has ever found it. No museum holds it. Every "photograph" of it is an illustration. What does exist is the text: about fourteen short lines, translated from Arabic into Latin in the twelfth century. It became perhaps the most quoted scripture of European alchemy. Isaac Newton translated it, and its second sentence, "that which is below is like that which is above", is now repeated as the slogan "as above, so below". This entry traces the text's documented history, gives the standard Latin with our own line-by-line translation, and separates the tablet of legend from the texts that are real, and from a twentieth-century book that borrowed its name. The earliest datable version is Arabic. The oldest source that can be dated is the Kitāb sirr al-khalīqa (Book of the Secret of Creation), attributed to Balīnūs. It is a compilation usually placed between about 750 and 850 CE, and some scholars tie it to the reign of the caliph al-Ma'mūn (813–833). That date is not certain. A second early Arabic version appears in a work attributed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān, the Kitāb Usṭuqus al-Uss al-Thānī (Second Book of the Element of the Foundation). Jābir is the legendary figure behind a large Arabic alchemical corpus whose own dating and authorship are debated. Earlier origins are hypothesis, not evidence. The Tablet is attributed to Hermes Trismegistus ("thrice-greatest Hermes"), the Greek-Egyptian figure behind the Hermetic literature of late antiquity. No Greek, Coptic, Syriac or Egyptian original has ever been found. Some scholars have argued for a lost Greek or Syriac source behind the Arabic. Others think it was composed in Arabic in the form we have. This is open. Latin Europe received it in the twelfth century. The Spanish translator Hugo of Santalla rendered the Sirr al-khalīqa into Latin, Tablet included. Another Latin version travelled with the enormously popular Secretum secretorum. From these came the version now called the "vulgate", the form printed in Nuremberg in 1541 (in the edition of Chrysogonus Polydorus) that became standard. The legend kept growing. Later European retellings moved the discovery to other finders, among them Alexander the Great and even Sarah, the wife of Abraham, in Hermes' tomb. These are legends about the text, not history. The Latin below is the standard vulgate text, public domain. The English is this archive's own line-by-line working translation, kept close to the Latin so that its obscurities are…

title: The Shroud of Turin
summary: A 4.4-metre linen bearing the faint negative-like image of a crucified man — documented from the 1350s, radiocarbon-dated to 1260–1390, its image still unexplained. Every test and every challenge, set side by side, with the Church's own distinction between icon and relic.
text: Vault entry V04 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Chapel of the Shroud, Cathedral of St John the Baptist, Turin; owned by the Holy See since 1983 · Recently added — pending full review. On the evening of 28 May 1898, an amateur photographer named Secondo Pia developed a glass plate in his darkroom in Turin. He had just been allowed to photograph a long, yellowed strip of linen displayed above the cathedral altar. On it was the faint, straw-coloured image of a man, front and back, laid head to head. When the negative emerged in the developing bath, Pia saw something he had not expected. The dark-and-light values of the cloth's image were reversed on the plate, and the reversal looked like a more natural face, the way an ordinary photograph looks. The image on the cloth, in other words, behaves like a negative. That discovery, made more than five centuries after the cloth's first documented appearance, turned a medieval relic into a modern scientific problem, and it has not been settled since. This entry sets out what the cloth physically is, what its documented history is, what every major test has found, and where the evidence genuinely points. It keeps faith in the cloth, the laboratory results and the unresolved puzzles as three separate things. The Shroud is a single piece of linen, about 4.4 metres long and 1.1 metres wide, woven in a 3-over-1 herringbone twill, a relatively elaborate weave. A narrow strip runs along one long edge, joined by a seam. On the cloth are: - a faint body image, frontal and dorsal, of a bearded man with his hands crossed. The image is extremely superficial, affecting only the top fibres of the threads; - reddish stains in the places associated with the wounds of crucifixion: wrists, feet, side, scalp and back; - two long lines of scorch marks and holes from a fire in 1532, when the folded cloth was damaged inside its silver reliquary; - water stains from the same fire; - until 2002, about thirty patches sewn on by the Poor Clare nuns of Chambéry in 1534, together with a backing cloth. Sources count them slightly differently. - c. 1354–1355, Lirey (France). The cloth first appears in the historical record in the collegiate church founded by the knight Geoffroi de Charny. A lead pilgrim's badge found in Paris (now in the Musée de Cluny) shows a long cloth with a double body image and the arms of the Charny and Vergy families. It is physical evidence that the cloth was being shown to pilgrims. How Charny came to own it is not recorded. - 1389. Pierre d'Arcis, bishop of Troyes, wrote a memorandum to the Avignon pope Clement VII. He said that an earlier bishop had investigated the cloth and that an artist had confessed to painting it. Clement allowed the showings to continue on the condition that it be announced as a "figure or representation" and not as the true shroud. The memorandum is a real document. Whether its claim is accurate is contested, because no artist is named and the investigation's records do not survive. - 1453. Margaret de Charny passed the cloth to Duke Louis I of Savoy. It became a dynastic treasure of the House of Savoy. - 1532–1534. Fire at Chambéry; the Poor Clare nuns carried out the repairs. -…

title: The Holy Lance (“Spear of Destiny”)
summary: One Gospel sentence, four rival spearheads, and a 1970s occult myth. The Habsburg lance's gold sleeve reads LANCEA ET CLAVVS DOMINI, but metallurgy dates the blade centuries after the Crucifixion, and the 'Spear of Destiny' Hitler legend traces to a single 1972 book.
text: Vault entry V05 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Rival relics in Vienna (Imperial Treasury, Hofburg), Rome (St Peter's), and Vagharshapat, Armenia (Etchmiadzin); a copy in Kraków · Recently added — pending full review. In a glass case in the Imperial Treasury of the Hofburg palace in Vienna lies an iron spearhead about half a metre long. Its blade was broken long ago and has been bound together with a sleeve of silver, and over that, a sleeve of gold. Down its centre, set into an opening in the blade, is a slender iron pin, venerated as a nail from the Cross. On the gold sleeve, added for the emperor Charles IV in the fourteenth century, is an inscription: LANCEA ET CLAVVS DOMINI, "the lance and nail of the Lord." For a thousand years this object was part of the regalia of the Holy Roman Empire. It was carried before German kings, invoked in battle, and treated as the spear that pierced Christ's side on the cross. It is not the only claimant. Rome, Armenia and the memory of the First Crusade each hold, or once held, a "Holy Lance." Then, in 1972, a popular occult book gave the Vienna spear a new name and a new legend: the "Spear of Destiny", supposedly the object of Adolf Hitler's obsession. This entry separates the four spears from one another, and all of them from the myth. Only one Gospel mentions the lance. John 19:34: ἀλλ᾽ εἷς τῶν στρατιωτῶν λόγχῃ αὐτοῦ τὴν πλευρὰν ἔνυξεν, καὶ ἐξῆλθεν εὐθὺς αἷμα καὶ ὕδωρ. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance, and at once blood and water came out. The soldier is unnamed in John. The name Longinus (probably formed from the Greek lonchē, "lance") appears later, in the apocryphal Acts of Pilate (Gospel of Nicodemus) and in later tradition. That tradition turned him into a convert and a saint. Everything after the Gospel sentence is tradition, not scripture. 1. The Vienna lance (the Holy Lance of the Holy Roman Empire). - What it is. A winged spearhead of Carolingian type. Scientific examination has placed its making in the early medieval period, not the first century. The metallurgist Robert Feather, who was allowed to remove the sleeves in 2003, dated it to around the seventh century. More recent imaging studies reported in 2025 point to the eighth century. - Its history. It is documented among the insignia of the Ottonian kings in the tenth century, and Otto I is said to have carried it at the Battle of Lechfeld (955). Over time it was identified with the lance of St Maurice, the lance of Constantine and finally the lance of Longinus. The gold sleeve was added under Charles IV (mid-fourteenth century). It is the object of a documented cult, but its identification with the Gospel lance is a medieval tradition, not a finding. - Kraków. The cathedral keeps a copy of the Vienna lance. By tradition it was a gift from Emperor Otto III to Bolesław I of Poland around 1000. 2. The Vatican lance. - A lance-point venerated at Constantinople was described by pilgrims for centuries. Parts of it reportedly went to Paris with King Louis IX's purchases of Passion relics in the thirteenth century; those parts were lost in the French Revolution. - The remaining portion passed to the Ottomans after 1453. In 1492…

title: The Crown of Thorns
summary: A ring of bundled rushes bound with gold thread, with no thorns left on it, for which Saint Louis paid almost half his annual revenue and built the Sainte-Chapelle. Traced from the Gospel mockery through Constantinople, Venice and the Revolution to the night Notre-Dame burned.
text: Vault entry V06 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Notre-Dame de Paris (axial chapel) · Recently added — pending full review. On the evening of 15 April 2019, as the roof of Notre-Dame de Paris burned, the chaplain of the Paris fire brigade, Father Jean-Marc Fournier, went into the cathedral with firefighters to bring out its treasures. Among the objects carried to safety was a circlet about the size of a dinner plate, sealed in a ring of crystal and gold. Inside it was no thorn at all, only a ring of bundled rushes bound with gold thread. It is the object that King Louis IX of France bought for a sum close to half his annual revenue, and for which he built one of the most beautiful buildings in Europe. It is venerated as the Crown of Thorns placed on Jesus' head before his crucifixion. This entry follows the crown from the Gospel text to the fire. It separates the documented chain of ownership, which runs from the thirteenth century, from the earlier tradition, which cannot be traced object by object. The crowning with thorns appears in Mark (15:17), Matthew (27:29) and John (19:2): Καὶ οἱ στρατιῶται πλέξαντες στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν ἐπέθηκαν αὐτοῦ τῇ κεφαλῇ, καὶ ἱμάτιον πορφυροῦν περιέβαλον αὐτόν. And the soldiers wove a crown of thorns and put it on his head, and they clothed him in a purple robe. In the Gospels the crown is mockery: a parody of royal insignia placed on a man condemned as "King of the Jews". None of the Gospels records what became of it. - Late antiquity and Byzantium. Pilgrim accounts from late antiquity mention a crown of thorns venerated in Jerusalem. Later, a crown was kept among the Passion relics of the Byzantine emperors in Constantinople. The continuity between these and the Paris relic cannot be demonstrated object by object. It is a tradition of succession, not a chain of receipts. - 1238. The Latin emperor of Constantinople, Baldwin II, was desperate for money. His barons had pledged the crown to Venetian lenders. Baldwin turned to Louis IX, who paid off the debt. Sources give the sum as 135,000 livres tournois, close to half the royal budget. - 1239. Two Dominican friars escorted the relic to France. Louis received it in person, by the accounts barefoot and in penitential dress, and brought it to Paris. - 1242–1248. Louis built the Sainte-Chapelle in his palace on the Île de la Cité as a walk-in reliquary for the crown and his other Passion relics. Most of its walls are stained glass. - French Revolution. The Sainte-Chapelle's treasury was dispersed and many reliquaries were melted down. The crown survived and was placed in the Bibliothèque nationale. In 1806 it was given to Notre-Dame. - 2019. It was rescued from the fire and kept for safety at the Louvre. - December 2024. At the cathedral's reopening it was returned to Notre-Dame in a new reliquary designed by Sylvain Dubuisson, installed in the axial chapel behind the choir. It is shown for veneration on set days. What Paris holds is a circlet of rushes, a ring of bundled plant stems about 21 cm across, held together by gold thread. It has no thorns. Over the centuries individual thorns were detached and given as gifts by Byzantine emperors and French kings. That is…

title: The Ark of the Covenant
era: The Vault · The Early Iron Age
summary: The most precisely described object in the Bible, measured to the half-cubit, and one found nowhere. What the texts say it was and did, the four traditions of its fate (Babylon, Mount Nebo, beneath the Temple, Aksum), and what archaeology can and cannot add.
text: Vault entry V07 · Relics & Sacred Objects · No surviving object is verified; the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church holds that it is kept at Aksum · Recently added — pending full review. It may be the most precisely described object in the Bible. Exodus 25 gives its measurements to the half-cubit, its wood, its gold, its rings and poles, and the two golden cherubim facing each other across its lid with their wings spread. Priests carried it into the Jordan and around Jericho. Philistines captured it, and it was brought back. David danced before it. Solomon installed it in the innermost room of the Temple. Then, somewhere between Solomon and the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE, it drops out of the record. When the Roman general Pompey forced his way into the Holy of Holies of the rebuilt Temple in 63 BCE, the Roman historian Tacitus says he found the shrine empty. Josephus describes the innermost room of that Temple as holding nothing at all. This entry sets out what the texts say the Ark was and did, what the traditions say became of it, and what archaeology can and cannot say. It includes the claim, held with great seriousness by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, that it rests today in a chapel in Aksum. Exodus 25:10, in Hebrew: ועשו ארון עצי שטים אמתים וחצי ארכו ואמה וחצי רחבו ואמה וחצי קמתו They shall make an ark of acacia wood: two cubits and a half its length, a cubit and a half its width, and a cubit and a half its height. The rest of Exodus 25:10–22 specifies: - the box is to be overlaid with pure gold inside and out, with a gold moulding; - four gold rings hold two acacia poles overlaid with gold, and the poles are never to be removed (25:15); - a lid of pure gold, the kapporet (traditionally "mercy seat"); - two cherubim of hammered gold at its ends, facing each other, their wings overshadowing the lid; - the "testimony" is to be placed inside, meaning the tablets of the covenant. God says: "There I will meet with you, and from above the kapporet, from between the two cherubim, I will speak with you" (25:22). Its dimensions in modern terms. A cubit was a forearm's length, and ancient cubits varied. Using a common cubit of about 44.5 cm, the Ark measures roughly 111 × 67 × 67 cm. Using a longer "royal" cubit of about 52.5 cm, it measures roughly 131 × 79 × 79 cm. Either way it is a chest about the size of a large trunk, not a monumental object. The exact cubit intended is uncertain. The texts do not fully agree: - Deuteronomy 10 and 1 Kings 8:9: "There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone." - Hebrews 9:4, a first-century Christian text: the Ark held the tablets, a golden jar of manna and Aaron's rod that budded. This draws on traditions in Exodus 16 and Numbers 17, where those items are placed before the testimony rather than inside it. - It led the march through the wilderness and stopped the Jordan so Israel could cross (Joshua 3). It was carried around Jericho (Joshua 6). - It stood at the sanctuary at Shiloh. It was captured by the Philistines at the battle of Ebenezer (1 Samuel 4). In their temple the image of Dagon fell before it, and plague followed it from city to city until the Philistines sent…

title: The Nag Hammadi Codices
summary: Thirteen leather-bound papyrus books found in a sealed jar in 1945: the Gospel of Thomas, Sethian and Valentinian scriptures, Hermetic tractates, even a scrap of Plato. What the library is, what it isn't, and who may have buried it.
text: Vault entry V08 · Manuscripts & Codices · Coptic Museum, Cairo · Recently added — pending full review. In December 1945, near the Upper Egyptian town of Nag Hammadi, a farmer named Muhammad Ali al-Samman and his brothers were digging for sabakh, a nitrate-rich soil used as fertiliser, at the foot of the cliff called Jabal al-Tarif. They uncovered a sealed clay jar about a metre tall. By Muhammad Ali's later account, he hesitated to break it, fearing a jinn inside, then smashed it and found no gold, only leather-bound books of papyrus. The find passed through village hands, antiquities dealers and a family feud before the books reached scholars. What they held was the largest discovery of lost early Christian writings ever made: twelve codices and eight leaves of a thirteenth, containing some fifty-two texts, most of them unknown for sixteen centuries. - Thirteen codices (the thirteenth survives only as eight leaves tucked inside another), written in Coptic, the last stage of the Egyptian language, in Greek-derived letters. Most of the texts are translations of Greek originals. - Books of papyrus in leather covers, among the oldest surviving bound books. - Dating. Scraps of used papyrus (cartonnage) glued inside the covers to stiffen them include dated letters and receipts from the 340s CE. The books were therefore bound after the mid-fourth century. The texts themselves are older. Many are thought to have been composed in Greek in the second and third centuries. - The codices are kept in the Coptic Museum in Cairo, apart from a fragment elsewhere. The full photographic facsimile edition was published between 1972 and 1977. Who buried them, and why, is not known. A widely repeated hypothesis links them to monks of the nearby Pachomian monasteries. It suggests that they hid their books after Archbishop Athanasius's Easter letter of 367, which listed the approved books of scripture. This is plausible but unproven. Some scholars have argued instead for private owners, for an ancient burial custom, or for a library that belonged to no monastery at all. The library is not one school's scripture. It gathers texts of several kinds: - Sethian Gnostic texts, which tell of a transcendent God, a flawed creator (the Demiurge, often called Yaldabaoth) and the heavenly Seth: the Apocryphon of John (in three copies), Hypostasis of the Archons and Trimorphic Protennoia. - Valentinian texts: the Gospel of Truth and the Gospel of Philip. - The Gospel of Thomas, 114 sayings attributed to Jesus. Some parallel the canonical Gospels and many do not. Greek fragments of it had been found at Oxyrhynchus decades earlier without anyone knowing what they were. - Hermetic texts, including a Coptic version of part of the Asclepius and the previously unknown Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth. - Even a garbled Coptic translation of a passage of Plato's Republic. A few lines that have become famous, in this archive's own working renderings from the Coptic as published in the standard editions: Gospel of Thomas, opening (Codex II): These are the hidden sayings that the living Jesus spoke, and Didymos Judas Thomas wrote them down. Gospel of Thomas, saying 77: Split a piece of…

title: The Codex Gigas (“Devil's Bible”)
summary: The largest surviving medieval manuscript (92 cm tall, about 75 kg), with a Bible, Josephus, Isidore, medicine, exorcisms, and a full-page devil facing the Heavenly City. Plundered from Prague in 1648 and thrown from a burning castle in 1697. The legend of the walled-up monk, and what the script says instead.
text: Vault entry V09 · Manuscripts & Codices · National Library of Sweden (Kungliga biblioteket), Stockholm · Recently added — pending full review. It takes two people to lift it. Bound in wooden boards covered with leather and metal fittings, the Codex Gigas ("giant book") is about 92 centimetres tall, 50 wide and 22 thick, and weighs around 75 kilograms. It is the largest surviving medieval manuscript. Open it towards the end and you reach a page found in no other Bible: a full-page devil, nearly a metre high, green-faced, horned, clawed, crouching in an ermine loincloth. On the facing page is a Heavenly City. The pairing gave the book its nickname, the Devil's Bible, and a legend that has never let go of it. - 310 leaves of vellum survive. The count and the collation suggest that some leaves are missing. - Written in Bohemia in the early thirteenth century, usually dated around 1204–1230, probably at the Benedictine monastery of Podlažice. A note in a calendar in the book records a "Hermann the Recluse" (Hermannus inclusus), who is often taken to be its scribe. - One hand? Palaeographers have observed that the script is remarkably uniform throughout, and many conclude that a single scribe wrote it over many years. Estimates run to two decades or more. - Ownership. It passed from Podlažice to other Bohemian monasteries and then to the collections of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague, the same court that owned the Voynich Manuscript (V01). In 1648, at the end of the Thirty Years' War, the Swedish army took it as plunder. In 1697 a fire struck the royal castle in Stockholm, and the codex was reportedly thrown from a window to save it. It has been in the National Library of Sweden ever since, apart from loans home to Prague (2007–2008). The Codex is a library in one volume. Its contents include: - The Old Testament (Vulgate). - Josephus, Jewish Antiquities and The Jewish War, in Latin. - Isidore of Seville, Etymologies, an encyclopaedia of the medieval world. - Medical texts, including works of the Salernitan school. - The New Testament. - The Devil and the Heavenly City. - Cosmas of Prague, Chronicle of the Bohemians. - Confessions, penitential texts and exorcism formulae, including spells against illness and theft. - A calendar with necrology, listing names of the dead to be remembered. The best-known story says a monk who had broken his vows was sentenced to be walled up alive. To escape the sentence he promised to write, in one night, a book to glorify the monastery. At midnight, failing, he prayed to the devil, who finished the book and was rewarded with his portrait. The story is folklore. It is attested only long after the book was made and fits a common type of tale about pacts with the devil. The uniform script that makes the "single night" impossible is the same evidence that points to one scribe working for years. Devil and City, face to face. The devil page (page 290 in the library's numbering) sits directly after the penitential texts and faces the Heavenly City. The layout makes a theological statement: sin and salvation on facing pages, with confession standing between them. That is a documented reading of the book's structure. No hidden…

title: The Copper Scroll
summary: A Dead Sea Scroll punched into copper: 64 hiding places of silver and gold, sawn into 23 strips to be read, tagged with seven unexplained Greek letter-groups, and never once found.
text: Vault entry V10 · Texts & Tablets · The Jordan Museum, Amman · Recently added — pending full review. Most of the Dead Sea Scrolls (V02) are skins or papyri. In 1952, archaeologists in Qumran Cave 3 found two rolls of something else: copper, corroded so badly that they could not be unrolled. They had once been a single sheet about 2.4 metres long, inscribed by punching letters into the metal. For three years nobody could read them. In 1955–56, at the Manchester College of Science and Technology, the engineer Henry Wright Baker built a device to cut the rolls into 23 curved strips. The philologist John Allegro was involved in the project. When the strips were read, the text turned out to be unlike anything else from Qumran. It was a plain list of places where treasure was hidden. - Catalogued as 3Q15, the fifteenth item from Cave 3. It is now in the Jordan Museum, Amman. - The text lists about 64 locations: in ruins, cisterns, tombs, under steps and beside aqueducts. Each gives a depth in cubits and a quantity of silver, gold, vessels or scrolls. The totals run into many tonnes of precious metal. - The Hebrew is closer to the later Mishnaic language than to the literary Hebrew of most scrolls. The engraving is inexpert, and the text has spelling oddities that complicate reading. - Seven of the entries are followed by groups of two or three Greek letters, recorded in the editions as ΚΕΝ, ΧΑΓ, ΗΝ, ΘΕ, ΔΙ, ΤΡ, ΣΚ. The first entry, in a working rendering after the published translations: In the ruin in the Valley of Achor, under the steps that go eastward, forty cubits: a chest of silver and its vessels, a weight of seventeen talents. Every explanation has serious defenders and serious problems: - Real treasure of the Jerusalem Temple, hidden before the Roman siege of 70 CE. That would explain the quantities, but the amounts are enormous. - Treasure connected with the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 CE), if the scroll is later than the other Cave 3 finds. - A folkloric or literary list, along the lines of legends about hidden Temple vessels. The deadpan administrative style makes this seem less likely to many readers. - Not connected with the Qumran community at all. Its language and material stand apart from the other scrolls. No treasure from the list has ever been found. Many place-names cannot be identified with confidence, and searches since the 1960s, including Allegro's own expedition, found nothing. The Greek letter-groups. Seven entries are tagged with Greek letters in an otherwise Hebrew text. They have been read as abbreviations of names, perhaps of the people responsible for each cache (for example ΔΙ for a name like Didymos), as numerals, or as cues for a companion document. The scroll itself refers to "another writing" giving further details. One popular book claimed the letters spell out the name of the Egyptian pharaoh Akhenaten. That reading has no scholarly support. The letter-groups are real and deliberate. Their meaning is unknown. Metal as permanence. Choosing copper over leather for this one document looks like a deliberate choice of durability. The list was meant to outlast the people who made it. The Dead Sea Scrolls (V02)…

title: The Rohonc Codex
summary: 448 small pages in an unknown script of about 200 signs, with crucifixions beside crescents. Given to the Hungarian Academy in 1838, it is suspected as a forger's hoax and proposed as a coded prayer book. Every reading so far, and why none has held.
text: Vault entry V11 · Manuscripts & Codices · Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Budapest · Recently added — pending full review. In 1838 the Hungarian nobleman Count Gusztáv Batthyány gave his family library to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences. Among the thirty thousand volumes was a small book, about 12 by 10 centimetres, of 448 paper pages. It was written right to left in a script of about two hundred distinct signs, and it had 87 drawings: crucifixions, a Last Supper, soldiers, and symbols that look Christian, pagan and Islamic by turns. It had come from the library at Rohonc (today Rechnitz, in Austria). Nearly two centuries later, it is still unread. - 448 pages of paper. Watermarks have been matched to Venetian paper of the sixteenth century (roughly the 1520s–1540s). That dates the paper, not the writing. - Around 200 signs. That is too many for an alphabet and too few for a logographic script such as Chinese. The number points to a syllabary, a mixed system, or a cipher with abbreviation symbols. - Direction. The text appears to run right to left, judging from where lines break and where the pictures sit. - Illustrations include Christian scenes alongside a crescent and a cross drawn together. - The hoax hypothesis. The historian Károly Szabó proposed in the nineteenth century that it was forged by Sámuel Literáti Nemes, a Transylvanian antiquarian known to have produced documented forgeries in the 1830s. The sixteenth-century paper does not rule this out, because old blank paper could be used, but the sheer length of the book and its internal consistency make a hoax harder to sustain. - Claimed readings. Over the years people have proposed that it is Old Hungarian (Székely runes), Dacian, Brahmi-derived, Sumerian and more. None has survived scrutiny. - The most serious recent work. In 2018, in the journal Cryptologia, Levente Zoltán Király and Gábor Tokai argued that the codex is a coded Christian devotional text, something like a breviary. They proposed that it paraphrases New Testament passages and uses an invented cipher-script with many abbreviation signs, and they suggested a late-sixteenth-century date. Their analysis identified numerals and the structure of some passages but did not produce a full reading. Signs beside pictures. The drawings of Gospel scenes give readers anchors. Where a crucifixion appears, the nearby text is probably about the Passion. That is how the 2018 study proposed its Christian reading. It is a real method, similar to reading a bilingual inscription, but it produces hypotheses rather than translations. Cross and crescent together. Drawings that combine Christian and Islamic symbols have fed theories of a Dacian, Cuman or "syncretic" origin. For a book from Ottoman-bordering Hungary, the combination may simply reflect the world its author lived in. The meaning of those images is open. The Voynich Manuscript (V01) and the Book of Soyga (V19), which are other unread or disputed scripts, and the Reformation-era Christianity of Central Europe (ch31). What's well supported by the evidence - A 448-page paper codex in an unknown script of about 200 signs, with 87 illustrations, given to the Hungarian…

title: The Ketef Hinnom Silver Scrolls
era: The Vault · The Early Iron Age
summary: Two tiny silver amulets from a Jerusalem tomb, excavated in 1979 and unrolled over three years, carrying the Priestly Blessing (‘May YHWH bless you and keep you’). They are about four centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls and the oldest known artefacts bearing words also found in the Bible.
text: Vault entry V12 · Texts & Tablets · The Israel Museum, Jerusalem · Recently added — pending full review. In 1979, on a slope overlooking Jerusalem's Hinnom Valley, a thirteen-year-old volunteer on Gabriel Barkay's excavation was clearing a burial cave. A collapsed ceiling had sealed its lowest chamber, and it had escaped the looting that emptied the rest. Among the finds, with pottery, jewellery and arrowheads, were two tiny rolled strips of silver. The larger was under 10 centimetres long when unrolled, and the smaller about 4. They were amulets, meant to be worn on a cord. Unrolling them without destroying them took three years. Inside, scratched into the silver in the old Hebrew script, was the divine name YHWH and words that anyone who knows the Hebrew Bible recognises: "May YHWH bless you and keep you." - Two silver amulets, known as KH1 and KH2, from Cave 25 at Ketef Hinnom ("shoulder of Hinnom"). - Letters were incised in palaeo-Hebrew script. The writing is faint and damaged, and parts of both texts are reconstructed. - Dating. Barkay first dated them on palaeographic grounds to the late seventh century BCE, then revised this towards the early sixth, just before the Babylonian destruction of 586 BCE. A new edition using advanced imaging (Barkay, Vaughn, Lundberg and Zuckerman, BASOR, 2004) supported a pre-exilic date. A few scholars have argued for a later, Hellenistic date. Most specialists accept the late Iron Age. Both amulets carry a form of the Priestly Blessing of Numbers 6:24–26. The biblical text, in the Masoretic tradition: יברכך יהוה וישמרך May YHWH bless you and keep you; יאר יהוה פניו אליך ויחנך may YHWH make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you; ישא יהוה פניו אליך וישם לך שלום may YHWH lift up his face to you and give you peace. The amulets' own wording is shorter and not identical. KH2, for example, preserves a version that moves from the blessing of the first line to "and give you peace". The difference matters. It shows the blessing circulating in a slightly different form from the later standard text. These are the oldest known artefacts carrying a text also found in the Hebrew Bible, about four centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls (V02). They show that this blessing, and the use of YHWH in personal protection, was current in Jerusalem before the Babylonian exile. They do not show that the Book of Numbers as a whole existed then. That wider question is open. Words as protection. Rolled up and worn on the body, the blessing becomes an apotropaic object, one that guards against harm. The amulets also contain phrases about rebuking evil. This is an early physical case of what later Judaism formalised in the tefillin and mezuzah: scripture worn and fixed in place for protection. The old script. Palaeo-Hebrew is the script later reserved for the divine name in some Dead Sea Scrolls (V02). Here it is simply the ordinary writing of its time. The script's later role as a sacred marker grew out of this everyday use. Pre-exilic Israel (ch07), the Dead Sea Scrolls (V02), the Ark of the Covenant (V07), and the Priestly Blessing's continuing use in synagogue and church liturgy (ch19, ch16). What's well supported by…

title: The Tilma of Guadalupe
summary: The cloak venerated as Juan Diego's, bearing the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe. It was attacked in 1556 as 'painted by an Indian, Marcos', survived a bomb in 1921, and was studied in infrared in 1979. The Nahuatl account, the documents, the science and the myths, kept apart.
text: Vault entry V13 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mexico City · Recently added — pending full review. Above the altar of the modern Basilica of Guadalupe, behind glass, hangs a length of coarse cloth about 1.7 metres tall. On it is the image of a young woman with a dark, gentle face, hands joined, standing on a crescent moon and wrapped in a blue-green mantle scattered with stars. She is surrounded by golden rays and held up by an angel. The Church calls her Our Lady of Guadalupe. Millions of pilgrims come to see her every year. The cloth is venerated as the tilma (cloak) of Juan Diego, an Indigenous convert. According to the tradition, in December 1531 the image appeared on it when he opened the cloak before the bishop of Mexico and let fall the roses he had been told to gather on the hill of Tepeyac. - The account. The classic narrative is the Nican Mopohua ("Here it is told"), written in Nahuatl. It tells of four apparitions to Juan Diego, the Virgin's request for a church, the bishop's demand for a sign, and the roses in December. - Its date. The Nican Mopohua was first printed in 1649 by Luis Lasso de la Vega, as part of the Huei tlamahuiçoltica. Most scholars attribute its composition to the Indigenous scholar Antonio Valeriano (c. 1520–1605), which would place it in the sixteenth century. The date and authorship are debated. - Its most famous line. In the Virgin's words to Juan Diego: Cuix amo nican nica nimonantzin? "Am I not here, I who am your mother?" - 1556. Archbishop Alonso de Montúfar promoted the devotion at the shrine of Tepeyac. The Franciscan Francisco de Bustamante preached against it, saying the image had been "painted yesterday by an Indian, Marcos". This is usually identified as Marcos Cipac de Aquino, a known Indigenous painter. The archbishop's inquiry (Información of 1556) is a real document. It proves that the image and its cult existed by 1556, and it proves that its origin was disputed even then. - 1648–1649. The first printed accounts appeared: Miguel Sánchez in Spanish (1648) and Lasso de la Vega in Nahuatl (1649). - 1921. A bomb hidden in flowers beneath the image exploded. The image was undamaged, while a bronze altar crucifix was bent by the blast. The crucifix is still displayed. - 1996–2002. The long-time abbot of the Basilica, Guillermo Schulenburg, doubted that Juan Diego was a historical person. A Vatican-appointed commission defended his historicity, and Juan Diego was canonised in 2002. Historians remain divided. - The fibre. The cloth is traditionally described as agave (ixtle) fibre. Some studies suggest other plant fibres, and no fibre analysis has been fully published under independent conditions. - Infrared study (1979, sometimes dated 1981). The biophysicist Philip Callahan photographed the image in infrared. He reported that the face, hands and robe showed no underdrawing and were not explained to his satisfaction. He also reported that the moon, the angel, the gold rays, the stars and parts of the mantle show signs of later additions and retouching with ordinary paints. Both findings are regularly cited, by opposite sides. - Popular claims that NASA found the image…

title: The Holy Grail
summary: The Gospels mention a cup and say nothing of its fate. The Grail was born in French romance around 1190. Valencia's agate cup, Genoa's glass dish and León's onyx chalice, set against the literature that made them sacred, and the modern 'bloodline' hoax.
text: Vault entry V14 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Claimants in Valencia, Genoa, León and elsewhere · Recently added — pending full review. In the Cathedral of Valencia, in a chapel of its own, stands a small cup of dark red agate, about 9 centimetres across. It is mounted on a gold stem with two curved handles and a base carved from an inverted cup of chalcedony. Pope John Paul II celebrated Mass with it in 1982, and Benedict XVI did the same in 2006, calling it "this most famous chalice". It is the most widely known of the objects venerated as the Holy Chalice, the cup of the Last Supper. It is not the only one. Around the world, perhaps two hundred places claim a Grail. What connects them all is not an ancient chain of custody but a set of stories written in France around the year 1200. - The Gospels. Jesus took "a cup" at the Last Supper (Mark 14:23; Matthew 26:27; Luke 22:17–20; 1 Corinthians 11:25). No Gospel says what became of it. - Chrétien de Troyes, Perceval, or the Story of the Grail (c. 1190). A mysterious graal, apparently a serving dish, is carried in procession in a castle. Chrétien does not say it is the cup of the Last Supper, and the poem breaks off unfinished. - Robert de Boron, Joseph d'Arimathie (late 12th / early 13th century). Here the Grail becomes the vessel of the Last Supper, used by Joseph of Arimathea to catch Christ's blood at the Cross and carried west by his family. - The Vulgate Cycle and Malory. The Grail quest becomes the spiritual summit of the Arthurian legend: Galahad's quest, the Fisher King, the wasteland. - Valencia (Santo Cáliz). The agate cup itself has been dated by some archaeologists to between the second century BCE and first century CE, from its style and workmanship. The mounting is medieval. Its documented history begins with a 1399 record at the monastery of San Juan de la Peña in Aragon. The link to the Last Supper is tradition. - Genoa (Sacro Catino). A hexagonal green dish, taken from Caesarea in 1101 during the First Crusade, once believed to be emerald. It was identified with the Grail only later. It proved to be glass, and it was broken after being taken to Paris under Napoleon. Modern study considers it Islamic glass of the ninth or tenth century. - León (Chalice of Doña Urraca). An onyx cup in a jewelled eleventh-century mounting, in the Basilica of San Isidoro. In 2014 two historians argued that it was the Grail, using medieval Egyptian texts. Most specialists rejected the argument. The Grail as symbol before object. In the romances the Grail stands for the Eucharist, divine grace, and a purity only the worthy can approach. The Fisher King's wound and the wasted land read as a kingdom's health bound to its king's spiritual state. This is the same logic as the archive's theme chapter on sacred kingship (ch49). Modern mythologies. Twentieth-century books reinterpreted the Grail as a bloodline ("San Graal" read as "sang réal", "royal blood") descending from Jesus and Mary Magdalene. That idea was popularised by The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail (1982) and The Da Vinci Code (2003). The "Priory of Sion" documents behind it were exposed as twentieth-century forgeries by their own creator. This…

title: The True Cross
summary: Wood venerated as the Cross in fourth-century Jerusalem, where deacons guarded it because a pilgrim once bit off a piece. Helena's discovery legend and Eusebius's silence, Calvin's 'shipload' and the 1870 attempt to measure every fragment.
text: Vault entry V15 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Fragments in churches worldwide; notable relics in Rome, Jerusalem, Mount Athos, Paris and elsewhere · Recently added — pending full review. Sometime in the 380s, a pilgrim from the western edge of the Roman world, a woman named Egeria, stood in Jerusalem on Good Friday and watched a ritual she described in a letter to the women of her community. The bishop sat at a table on Golgotha. A silver-gilt casket was opened, and pieces of wood were laid out. One by one the faithful came forward, bent down, touched the wood with their forehead and eyes, and kissed it. Deacons stood around the table and watched closely, because someone had once, Egeria reports, bitten off a piece and carried it away. This is one of the earliest eyewitness descriptions of the relic venerated as the True Cross. - The discovery legend. By the end of the fourth century, Christians told how Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, found the Cross in Jerusalem around 326–328. It lay beneath a pagan temple built over Golgotha by Hadrian. Bishop Ambrose of Milan tells the story in his funeral oration for the emperor Theodosius (395). Eusebius, a contemporary of Constantine and Helena, describes Helena's pilgrimage and Constantine's Church of the Holy Sepulchre but does not mention the finding of the Cross. That silence is often noted. - Variant legends. In other versions a Jew named Judas (later Judas Cyriacus) reveals where the Cross is, or the true cross is told apart from the two thieves' crosses by a healing miracle. These are legends. - Veneration in Jerusalem is well documented from the 380s (Egeria). The feast of the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) grew from the dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. - Distribution. Fragments were sent across the Christian world: to Rome (Santa Croce in Gerusalemme), Constantinople, and later to many medieval churches. The Persian king Khosrow II captured the Jerusalem relic in 614, and the emperor Heraclius restored it in 630. - Calvin's jibe (1543). In his Treatise on Relics, John Calvin wrote that if every fragment were gathered together, they would make "a good shipload", though one man had carried the cross. - Rohault de Fleury's count (1870). The French architect Charles Rohault de Fleury catalogued and measured the known fragments. He calculated that together they made up only a small fraction of the estimated volume of a Roman cross. That answers Calvin's arithmetic. It does not establish that any fragment is genuine. The cross as the central Christian sign. The cross became Christianity's defining symbol from the fourth century on, after Constantine. Relic, image and gesture (the sign of the cross) reinforce one another. The staurotheke. Reliquaries of the True Cross, often in the form of a double-barred cross, were made as theological objects. The famous Byzantine Limburg Staurotheke is one: gold, enamel and gems arranged as a map of heaven around the wood. The legend as art. The Legend of the True Cross traces the wood from Adam's grave to Helena's discovery. It became a great fresco cycle, most famously Piero della Francesca's at Arezzo (c. 1452–1466), and joins…

title: The James Ossuary
summary: A first-century bone box inscribed 'James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus'. It was declared a forgery by the Israel Antiquities Authority, and its owner was acquitted after an eight-year trial that proved nothing either way. One disputed phrase, and the odds behind common names.
text: Vault entry V16 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Returned to its private owner, Oded Golan, after a criminal trial · Recently added — pending full review. In October 2002, at a press conference in Washington, D.C., a limestone box about 50 centimetres long was presented to the world. It was an ossuary, a chest for bones of the kind Jews in and around Jerusalem used for secondary burial in the first century BCE and first century CE. Along one side ran a short Aramaic inscription: Ya'akov bar Yosef akhui di Yeshua, "James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus." If genuine, and if it referred to the Jesus of the Gospels, it would be the earliest physical reference to Jesus ever found. Within a year the Israel Antiquities Authority declared the inscription a forgery. Within two years the box's owner was on trial. The trial ended in 2012 with an acquittal that settled nothing about the inscription. - A limestone ossuary of the standard first-century type. The box itself is accepted as ancient. - The inscription, in Aramaic, carved into the side: יעקוב בר יוסף אחוי דישוע Ya'akov bar Yosef akhui di-Yeshua: James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus - The dispute centres on the second half, "brother of Jesus". Critics argued that it was added to a genuine but ordinary inscription ("James son of Joseph") and that a fake patina was applied to disguise the fresh cuts. - 2002. The ossuary was published by the epigrapher André Lemaire in Biblical Archaeology Review and exhibited at the Royal Ontario Museum, where it cracked in transit. - 2003. An Israel Antiquities Authority committee concluded that the inscription was forged, citing its study of the patina. - 2004–2012. The owner, the collector Oded Golan, and others were tried in Jerusalem on forgery charges covering this and other artefacts. In March 2012 the judge acquitted him of forging the ossuary inscription. The judge found that the prosecution had not proved forgery beyond reasonable doubt, and stated explicitly that the verdict did not prove the inscription authentic. Golan was convicted of lesser charges relating to trading in antiquities. - Afterwards. The ossuary was returned to Golan. Scholarly opinion remains divided. Some epigraphers and geologists defend the whole inscription, and others maintain that the second half is modern. Even if the whole inscription is ancient, James, Joseph and Jesus were all very common names in first-century Judaea. The identification with the family of Jesus of Nazareth therefore depends on probability arguments. One is that the unusual mention of a brother suggests the brother was notable. Those arguments are debated too. An inscription as a claim of identity. Ossuary inscriptions usually record name and father. Naming a brother is rare, and that rarity is exactly what makes this line either remarkable or suspicious. The text's significance lies entirely in one short phrase. The object shows how much weight a single line of writing can be made to carry. Early Christianity (ch16), Second Temple Judaism (ch10), and the forgery cases elsewhere in the Vault: the "Gospel of Jesus's Wife" (V17) and the forged Dead Sea Scroll fragments (V02). What's well supported by the…

title: The “Gospel of Jesus's Wife”
summary: A card-sized Coptic fragment in which Jesus says 'my wife', announced by a Harvard historian in 2012 and exposed by 2016: a text patched together from an online Gospel of Thomas, down to its typo. How a forgery is caught, step by step.
text: Vault entry V17 · Manuscripts & Codices · A papyrus fragment once studied at Harvard; now recognised as a modern forgery · Recently added — pending full review. In September 2012, at an international congress of Coptic studies in Rome, the Harvard historian Karen L. King presented a scrap of papyrus smaller than a business card. It had eight broken lines of Coptic on one side. In one of them Jesus says, "my wife…". King was careful. She said the fragment did not prove that Jesus was married, only that some early Christians may have discussed it. She provisionally titled it The Gospel of Jesus's Wife. The news travelled around the world within hours. Four years later, the fragment had become a textbook case of how forgeries are exposed, and King herself agreed that it was almost certainly fake. This entry is in the Vault because the method matters as much as the object. The standards that exposed it are the same standards this archive applies everywhere. - About 4 × 8 cm of papyrus, with eight incomplete lines in Sahidic Coptic on one side. - Its key phrases, in translation: "Jesus said to them, 'My wife…'" and "…she will be able to be my disciple…". - Provenance was supplied by the anonymous owner. It came with a typed contract and a note said to date from the 1980s, claiming the fragment came from a German collector. Both later proved false. 1. The text was patched together. Within days, the New Testament scholar Francis Watson showed that almost every phrase could be found in the Coptic Gospel of Thomas from Nag Hammadi (V08), cut up and reassembled. 2. A modern typo. The fragment reproduced a typographical error found in a 2002 online edition of the Gospel of Thomas by Michael Grondin. It was an error no ancient scribe could have copied. 3. A companion fragment. A second papyrus from the same owner, a fragment of the Gospel of John in Coptic, turned out to be copied line by line from a published 1924 edition of a different manuscript, with the same line breaks. 4. Material tests misread. Radiocarbon tests dated the papyrus to antiquity, and ink analysis did not rule out an ancient origin. But old blank papyrus is available to forgers, so an old material does not date the writing. That is the same point as the "parchment versus writing" question in the Voynich entry (V01). 5. The provenance collapsed. In 2016 the journalist Ariel Sabar, writing in The Atlantic, identified the owner as Walter Fritz, a former Egyptology student turned businessman. Fritz's documents did not hold up. Fritz denied forging the papyrus, but most scholars regard him as the likely forger. 6. King's response. King said that the evidence now "presses in the direction of forgery". Forgery as mirror. The fragment said what some modern readers wanted an ancient text to say, about women disciples and a married Jesus. A text that confirms a hope too neatly deserves the closest scrutiny. This is not because the hope is wrong, but because forgers write to hopes. The evidence pattern. A forgery was exposed by several independent lines of evidence: textual dependence, a modern error, a companion fake and provenance failure. No single test was decisive, but together they were…

title: Codex Sinaiticus
summary: The oldest complete New Testament, in a fourth-century Greek Bible now split among four libraries: London, Leipzig, Sinai and St Petersburg. It ends Mark at 16:8, includes Barnabas and Hermas, and still carries the dispute over how it left Mount Sinai.
text: Vault entry V18 · Manuscripts & Codices · British Library (London), Leipzig University Library, St Catherine's Monastery (Sinai), National Library of Russia (St Petersburg) · Recently added — pending full review. In 1844 the young German scholar Constantin von Tischendorf was visiting St Catherine's Monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai. By his own later account, which the monks have always disputed, he saw old parchment leaves in a basket and was told they were bound for the fire. He left with 43 leaves of an ancient Greek Bible and gave them to Leipzig. In 1859 he returned under the patronage of the Russian Tsar and was shown the rest. The manuscript went to St Petersburg. How it came to leave Sinai, whether as loan, gift or appropriation, is a dispute that has never been resolved. In 1933 the Soviet government, needing hard currency, sold most of it to the British Museum for £100,000. What they had found is the Codex Sinaiticus, written around 330–360 CE. It is one of the two oldest near-complete Bibles in the world, and it contains the oldest complete New Testament. - Originally over 730 leaves of fine parchment. About 400 survive, divided among four institutions: - British Library, London: 347 leaves, the main part. - Leipzig University Library: 43 leaves (1844). - St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai: 12 leaves and fragments, found in 1975 in a sealed room. - National Library of Russia: fragments of 3 leaves. - Written in Greek uncials, capital letters with no spaces between words (scriptio continua), in four columns per page for most books. - Several scribes, usually counted as three, and thousands of later corrections by many hands. The corrections are themselves a record of how the text was read over centuries. - In 2009 the four institutions completed the Codex Sinaiticus Project, reuniting the whole surviving manuscript online, with transcription. - The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), including books that later Protestant Bibles would call apocrypha, such as Tobit, Judith and 1 and 4 Maccabees. - The whole New Testament, together with two early Christian works later left out of the canon: the Epistle of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas. - Mark ends at 16:8, with the women fleeing the empty tomb "for they were afraid". The longer ending (Mark 16:9–20) that most later Bibles print is absent. That fact, shared with Codex Vaticanus, is central to modern textual study of Mark. Sacred names in shorthand. Like other early Christian manuscripts, Sinaiticus writes the holiest names as contractions with a line over them: ΘΣ for theos (God), ΚΣ for kyrios (Lord), ΙΣ for Iēsous, ΧΣ for Christos. These nomina sacra are a real, deliberate scribal marking of holiness. They are closely related to the way Jewish scribes set the divine name apart (V02). The text as a living layer-cake. The corrections, which run into the thousands, show later readers adjusting the text towards the form that later became standard. The manuscript preserves a text in motion, not a single fixed original. Early Christianity (ch16), Patristic Christianity (ch22, for the formation of the canon), the Dead Sea Scrolls (V02, for the Jewish scribal handling of the…

title: The Book of Soyga
summary: John Dee's book of magic, ending in 36 grids of letters he could never read. An angel told him only Michael could explain it. Rediscovered in 1994; in 2006 a cryptographer showed the grids are generated from seed words by a fixed rule, not hidden messages.
text: Vault entry V19 · Manuscripts & Codices · Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Bodley 908) and British Library (Sloane MS 8) · Recently added — pending full review. In 1583, at his house in Mortlake by the Thames, the Elizabethan mathematician and astrologer John Dee sat with his scryer Edward Kelley before a crystal stone. Dee, who spent much of his life trying to converse with angels, asked a question that had troubled him for years. What did his Book of Soyga mean? According to the diary in which Dee recorded these sessions, the angel Uriel answered that the book had been revealed to Adam in Paradise, and that only the archangel Michael could interpret it. Dee never found out what it meant. After his death the book dropped out of sight. For four centuries it was thought lost. - In 1994 the historian Deborah Harkness identified two copies under the title Aldaraia sive Soyga vocor ("Aldaraia, or I am called Soyga"): MS Bodley 908 in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, and Sloane MS 8 in the British Library. - Both are sixteenth-century Latin manuscripts of magic: lists of angelic and demonic names, astrological material and spells. - Each ends with 36 tables of letters, each a grid of 36 × 36 capitals (the Bodley copy crams them onto its last pages). They look like random noise. The tables were what defeated Dee. - The book likes reversals. Soyga is Agyos backwards, the Greek hagios, "holy". Lapis (stone) appears as Sipal, and Bonum (good) as Munob. In 2006 the mathematician and cryptographer Jim Reeds published a study showing that the tables are not random. Each is generated by a rule from a short seed word: a Latin name or word, laid down letter by letter and then expanded across the grid by a fixed arithmetic procedure applied to the letters. Given the seed and the rule, the whole table can be reproduced. Reeds reconstructed the method and recovered the seed words. That is a genuine decipherment of the tables' structure. It explains how they were made. It does not reveal any hidden message, because the tables were never a coded sentence. They are mechanically generated magical grids, a way of turning a holy word into a field of letters, in the tradition of letter squares such as the SATOR square and of Kabbalistic letter combinations. Letters as power. Soyga belongs to the Renaissance magia tradition that treated letters and names as channels of cosmic force. It draws on Kabbalah (ch26), including its Christian adaptations, and on the angel-names of the Liber Juratus and similar works. A grid generated from a holy word embodies the word across a surface. It is closer to a talisman than to a text meant for reading. Reversal as veiling. Writing words backwards is a real, documented habit of this manuscript. It is a simple concealment, a way of marking words as secret or sacred, and not a cipher. Kabbalah and its Christian adaptations (ch26), the Theosophical and occult revival (ch37, for Dee's later influence on the Golden Dawn), the Voynich Manuscript (V01, also once linked to Dee) and the Rohonc Codex (V11). What's well supported by the evidence - A sixteenth-century Latin magical manuscript, owned by John Dee, surviving in two copies identified in…

title: The Papyrus of Ani
summary: A 24-metre Book of the Dead made for the scribe Ani at Thebes. Its judgment scene, the heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at before the Devourer, is the most famous image of the afterlife from the ancient world. Spell 125 and the 42 denials of the Negative Confession.
text: Vault entry V20 · Manuscripts & Codices · British Museum, London (EA 10470) · Recently added — pending full review. A scribe named Ani stands with his wife Tutu in a hall of judgment. In the centre stands a balance. On one pan lies Ani's heart. On the other lies a single feather, the sign of Ma'at: truth, order, rightness. The jackal-headed Anubis checks the plumb line. The ibis-headed Thoth stands ready with his palette to record the verdict. Crouched beside the scales is Ammit, the "Devourer", part crocodile, part lion, part hippopotamus, waiting to eat any heart heavier than truth. This scene, painted in the thirteenth century BCE, is the most famous image of judgment after death from the ancient world. It comes from the Papyrus of Ani. - A roll of papyrus about 24 metres long, made for Ani, a royal scribe and overseer of offerings at Thebes. It dates to the 19th Dynasty, around 1250 BCE. - A copy of the "Book of Going Forth by Day", better known as the Book of the Dead. This is a collection of spells that helped the deceased pass through the dangers of the afterlife. The Papyrus of Ani is considered one of the finest surviving copies, and it has an unusually large number of painted vignettes. - Acquired in 1888 in Egypt by E. A. Wallis Budge for the British Museum, from the antiquities trade. Budge cut the roll into sheets for display and study, a practice modern conservators regret. The judgment scene illustrates Spell 125. There the deceased declares his innocence before Osiris and then, one by one, before forty-two divine judges, each named. He addresses each judge with a denial of one wrongdoing, which is why it is called the "Negative Confession". Among the denials, in this archive's working renderings: I have not robbed with violence. I have not killed man or woman. I have not stolen the offerings of the gods. I have not told lies. I have not caused anyone to weep. The standard of judgment is Ma'at, which is social as much as ritual: honesty, not cheating with weights and measures, not taking what belongs to others, not causing grief. The declarations are a documented ancient moral code in the first person. True of voice. If the heart balanced against the feather, the deceased was declared maa-kheru, "true of voice" or "justified". Thoth recorded the verdict, and the dead person could pass on to the realm of Osiris. Heart and feather. For Egyptians the heart (ib) was the seat of thought, memory and will, and it could testify against its owner. For that reason Spell 30B, often inscribed on heart scarabs placed on the mummy, commands the heart not to speak against the deceased. The feather is the hieroglyph for ma'at. The scene is a visual equation: a life is weighed against truth itself. Words that work. The Book of the Dead's spells were effective by being written. Hieroglyphs themselves were considered potent, and in some tombs dangerous signs, such as snakes and scorpions, were drawn cut in half so they could not harm the dead.
