It shows a people called Israel in Canaan before the monarchy described in the Bible, and it predates the Mesha (V22) and Tel Dan (V23) stelae by over three centuries. It says nothing about the Exodus, Moses, or where Israel came from. It is sometimes used on both sides of the Exodus debate, but it only shows Israel already present in Canaan by c. 1208. A minority of scholars have questioned the reading "Israel" (for instance proposing Jezreel), but the majority reading stands. Some scholars have also connected the stele with battle reliefs at Karnak that may show Merneptah's Canaan campaign, including a group sometimes identified as Israel; that identification is disputed. The king who restores order. Egyptian victory texts present the king as upholding Ma'at, cosmic order, against chaos. Foreign enemies are chaos personified, and their destruction is a ritual necessity as much as a military claim. The Nine Bows. Egypt's traditional enemies were symbolised as nine bows under the king's feet. The stele names them as crushed. The formula made every victory an act in a cosmic drama. Reused stone. Carving over an earlier king's stele was common. It borrowed the monument's sanctity…

title: The Pilate Stone
summary: A broken limestone block from Caesarea, reused as a step in the Roman theatre, which names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judaea. Found in 1961, it is the only inscription from Pilate's lifetime that names him, and it corrected the title later Roman writers gave him.
text: Vault entry V44 · Texts & Tablets · The Israel Museum, Jerusalem · Recently added — pending full review. In June 1961 an Italian team led by Antonio Frova was excavating the Roman theatre at Caesarea Maritima, the port city Herod the Great had built on the coast of Judaea. The archaeologist Maria Teresa Fortuna Canivet turned over a limestone block that had been used as a step in a later rebuilding of the theatre. Its underside carried four broken lines of Latin, and in the second line was a name known from every Christian creed: PILATVS. - A limestone block about 82 × 65 cm, cut down when it was reused, so that the left side of every line is missing. - The surviving text, with standard restorations in brackets: [ . . . ]S TIBERIEVM [ . . . PO]NTIVS PILATVS [ . . . PRAEF]ECTVS IVDA[EA]E [ . . . FE]CIT D[E . . . ] - It records that Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judaea, built or dedicated a Tiberieum, a structure named in honour of the emperor Tiberius. - Pilate governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE, so the stone dates from those years. The original is in the Israel Museum; a replica stands at Caesarea. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around 116, calls Pilate a procurator. So does most later tradition. The stone shows that in his own time Pilate's title was praefectus, a military rank. The governors of Judaea became procurators under Claudius, after Pilate's day. Tacitus used the title of his own time. The Gospels simply call him "governor" (Greek hēgemōn). The first line is the most uncertain. Proposals include: - a temple for the cult of the emperor, which Pilate, as a loyal official, would promote; - the epigrapher Géza Alföldy's restoration [Nautis] Tiberieum, "a Tiberieum for sailors": a lighthouse or harbour structure at Caesarea's port. Neither restoration can be proven from the surviving letters. Pilate appears in the four Gospels, in Josephus and Philo, who describe him as provocative and harsh, and in Tacitus, who notes that Christ "suffered the extreme penalty" under him. The stone adds no new events. What it gives is independent, contemporary confirmation of his office and name. A copper ring found at Herodium, inscribed "of Pilatus" and read with new imaging in 2018, may also be connected with him, although Pilatus was not a unique name. Honouring the emperor. Naming a building after Tiberius was a political and religious act. In the Roman world, loyalty to the emperor was expressed through cult. In Judaea this collided with Jewish law against images, and Josephus and Philo record Pilate provoking protests by bringing military standards and gilded shields into Jerusalem. Reuse as erasure. Cutting a governor's dedication down to serve as a stair shows how quickly monuments to officials lost their meaning. It also shows that the stone survived only by accident. Rome (ch13), Early Christianity (ch16) and Second Temple Judaism (ch10). Compare the James Ossuary (V16) for inscriptions naming New Testament figures and how they are tested, and the True Cross (V15). What's well supported by the evidence - A Latin dedication found at Caesarea in 1961 naming Pontius Pilate as praefectus of Judaea and a Tiberieum. It is authentic, from an…

title: The Nebra Sky Disc
summary: A bronze disc 30 cm across with a gold sun or full moon, a crescent and 32 stars, among them a cluster read as the Pleiades. It was dug up by looters in 1999, recovered in a Swiss police sting in 2002, and altered at least four times in antiquity. It may be the oldest known concrete depiction of the sky.
text: Vault entry V45 · Relics & Objects · State Museum of Prehistory, Halle (Saale) · Recently added — pending full review. In July 1999 two men with metal detectors, working illegally, dug into the summit of the Mittelberg, a hill near Nebra in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. They found a hoard: two bronze swords, two axes, a chisel, fragments of spiral bracelets, and a round green plate of bronze inlaid with gold. They sold it on, damaging it in the process. In February 2002, in a hotel in Basel, a buyer who said he represented a museum met the dealers. He was Harald Meller, the state archaeologist, working with the Swiss police. The disc was seized. The looters were later convicted, and one led archaeologists to the find spot. - A bronze disc about 30 cm across and about 2 kg, now green with corrosion, originally perhaps a dark brown or black-violet. - Inlaid with gold: a large circle (sun or full moon), a crescent, and 32 small circles read as stars, among them a tight group of seven, usually identified as the Pleiades. - Analysis of the metals suggests the copper came from the eastern Alps and the gold, at least in part, from Cornwall. That provenance has been debated but is widely accepted. - It went on the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2013. Close study shows the disc was altered several times. The interactive object steps through the stages: 1. Sun, moon and 32 stars. 2. Two horizon arcs are added at the edges; to fit them, one star is covered and two are moved. Each arc spans about 82°, close to the angle between the solstice sunsets (and sunrises) on the horizon at this latitude. 3. A curved band is added at the bottom, often read as a sun-boat. 4. About 39 holes are punched around the rim. 5. One arc is lost, and the disc is buried with the weapons and tools, around 1600 BCE. The hoard's swords and axes date the burial to the end of the Early Bronze Age, c. 1600 BCE, in the Únětice culture. In 2020, Rupert Gebhard and Rüdiger Krause argued that the looters' account of the find spot was unreliable, that the disc might not belong with the hoard, and that its style fits the Iron Age, a thousand years later. In 2021 Ernst Pernicka, Harald Meller and colleagues replied with soil, corrosion and metal analyses linking the disc to the hoard and the site. Most specialists accept the Bronze Age date, and the Iron Age proposal has few supporters. - A calendar? The horizon arcs track the sun between midsummer and midwinter. It has been proposed (notably by Rahlf Hansen) that the crescent and Pleiades together encode a rule for adding a leap month to keep lunar and solar years aligned. Such a rule is known from much later Babylonian texts. The idea is striking and debated. - A religious object? The boat, the sky and the burial with weapons suggest a sacred object, perhaps used by a ruler or priest, then deposited as an offering. - Both. In the Bronze Age, reading the sky and serving the gods were not separate. The sun-boat. The idea that the sun crosses the sky or the underworld in a boat is known from Egypt and from later Nordic Bronze Age rock carvings and razors. The band on the disc may be its earliest appearance in central Europe. Changing the…

title: The Piprahwa Relics
summary: Bone fragments, a soapstone urn and some 1,800 gems dug from a stupa in 1898 by a British estate manager. The urn's inscription says the shrine holds relics of the Buddha, or of the Buddha's kinsmen, depending on how it is read. In 2025 India halted a Sotheby's sale of the gems.
text: Vault entry V46 · Relics & Objects · Indian Museum, Kolkata; National Museum, New Delhi · Recently added — pending full review. In January 1898 William Claxton Peppé, an English estate manager in the Terai of northern India, near the Nepal border, had his workmen dig into a large brick mound on his land at Piprahwa. It was an ancient stupa. About 18 feet down they reached a massive sandstone coffer. Inside were five small vessels: urns and caskets of soapstone and crystal, holding bone fragments, ash, and some 1,800 tiny offerings: pearls, gems, gold leaf and stars, beads and shells. Around the lid of one urn ran a line of writing in the Brahmi script. It seemed to say that these were relics of the Buddha, enshrined by his own people, the Sakyas. The words are in a Prakrit language, and each can be glossed in the interactive object above. The standard reading: This deposit of relics of the Blessed One, the Buddha, is (the gift) of the Sakyas, the brothers of Sukiti, with their sisters, sons and wives. The grammar is ambiguous. The genitives can be arranged in more than one way. Soon after the find, the epigrapher J. F. Fleet argued that it could mean the relics of the Sakyas, the kinsmen of the Buddha. On that reading the bones are those of the Buddha's relatives, perhaps victims of the massacre of the Sakyas recorded in Buddhist tradition, and not the Buddha's own. Most scholars since have preferred the reading "relics of the Buddha", while accepting that the text can be taken both ways. The find came in the same years that a German archaeologist, Alois Führer, was exposed as a forger of Buddhist inscriptions and relics in the same region. Suspicion inevitably fell on Piprahwa. Investigations, including the historian Charles Allen's study (2008), concluded that Peppé's find was genuine and that Führer did not have the opportunity to plant it. Some doubts about the inscription's date have been raised, but most epigraphers accept it as ancient. In 1971–1973 the archaeologist K. M. Srivastava excavated deeper at Piprahwa and found earlier caskets with bone, and at the nearby monastery sealings reading "Kapilavastu", the name of the Buddha's home town. He argued that Piprahwa was Kapilavastu. Nepal identifies Kapilavastu with Tilaurakot, across the border, and the question remains disputed between the two countries. The British government kept most of the gems and gave the bone relics to King Chulalongkorn of Siam, who shared them among Buddhist communities in Asia. Much of the jewellery went to the Indian Museum in Calcutta (Kolkata). Peppé's family kept a share of the gems. In May 2025 Sotheby's in Hong Kong offered the family's gems for sale. The Indian government objected that they were sacred relics and national heritage. Buddhist leaders protested, and the sale was postponed. In July 2025 they were bought by the Godrej group and returned to India, where they are to be displayed. Relics and the stupa. Buddhist tradition says the Buddha's remains were divided into eight portions after his cremation, one of them to the Sakyas of Kapilavastu, each enshrined in a stupa. The stupa became the central monument of Buddhism, a mound whose relic core…

title: The Kensington Runestone
summary: A greywacke slab a Swedish immigrant farmer said he found under the roots of a tree in Minnesota in 1898, telling of Norse explorers killed in 1362. Scholars rejected it within months, and its runes and language point to the nineteenth century. It remains a beloved local symbol and a case study in how claims are tested.
text: Vault entry V47 · Texts & Tablets · Runestone Museum, Alexandria, Minnesota · Recently added — pending full review. In November 1898 Olof Öhman, a Swedish immigrant farmer near Kensington, Minnesota, was clearing trees on his land. According to his account, he pulled up an aspen and found a flat grey slab gripped in its roots. It weighed about 90 kg and was carved on its face and one edge with runes. Translated, they told of 8 Goths and 22 Norwegians on a journey of exploration from Vinland, of ten men found "red with blood and dead", a prayer to the Virgin, and a year: 1362. If genuine, Scandinavians had reached the middle of North America 130 years before Columbus. - In 1899 the stone was examined by Olaus Breda at the University of Minnesota and by scholars at the university in Christiania (Oslo). They declared it a modern forgery. - The objections were linguistic. The language is close to nineteenth-century Swedish, not fourteenth-century Norse. Some words and forms did not exist in 1362. Several runes are unusual or invented, and some match nineteenth-century runic alphabets in books a Swede of the period could own. - Hjalmar Holand, a writer and local historian, bought the stone in 1907 and spent half a century defending it. It was exhibited at the Smithsonian in 1948–49. - In 1967 two children of Öhman's neighbour John Gran said in a recorded interview that their father had made the stone with Öhman as a hoax. This is hearsay, and supporters reject it. From the 1980s the geologist Scott Wolter and the researcher Richard Nielsen argued that the carving's weathering implied great age, and that some runic forms, such as a dotted R, appear in medieval Scandinavian sources, including a manuscript from Gotland. Runologists such as Henrik Williams have answered that weathering estimates are unreliable for a stone of unknown history and that the language as a whole, not single letters, points to the nineteenth century. The overwhelming scholarly consensus is that the stone is a nineteenth-century creation. It remains a proud local symbol, standing at the Runestone Museum in Alexandria beside a giant statue of a Viking. The Vault includes objects whose claims are disproved as well as those that are proved or open. The Kensington stone is a clear case of how claims about ancient inscriptions are tested: by language, by script, by provenance and by weathering. It also shows how identity and pride keep a claim alive after the scholarly case has closed. Compare the Rök Runestone (V36), a genuine ninth-century inscription. "AVM, save from evil." The stone's one religious line invokes the Virgin Mary (AVM = Ave Maria). This is plausible in form for a medieval Catholic party. Critics note that such formulas were well known in the nineteenth century as well. Runes as heritage. For Scandinavian Americans in 1898, runes were a powerful symbol of ancestry. The late nineteenth century's romantic revival of the Viking past explains both why a forger might carve such a stone and why so many people wanted it to be true. Norse Paganism (ch23) and Native North American (ch62), whose lands are the setting of the claim. Compare the Rök Runestone (V36) and the…
